utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84bis-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, and Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for the day, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Good morning, Paul Rogers appearing for the Prosecutor together with Ms. Priya Gopalan and our case manager, Ms. Line Pedersen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rogers. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Ben Emmerson for Ramush Haradinaj, together with Rod Dixon, Annie O'Reilly, and Andrew Strong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Gregor Guy-Smith, Colleen Rohan, Chad Mair, and Gentian Zyberi on behalf of Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Richard Harvey on behalf of Lahi Brahimaj, assisted by Mr. Paul Troop, Ms. Sophie Rigney, and Ms. Rudina Jasini. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I propose we do this morning in relation to this witness is to bring him back in, see whether there's been any change of heart over the evening adjournment. It's quite possible that he may have reflected upon his position and now be more willing to answer questions. It may be that he isn't. We don't know. We have to wait and see. And then depending upon how he responds, I may take a further course of action which I've alerted my friends in relation to as to whether to treat him as an adverse witness. But we'll wait and see how he develops this morning. Now, unless my learned friends wish to object to that course of action, I rather we had the argument about it now than have any argument in front of the witness whilst he's sitting listening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, we don't have an application by you yet, Mr. Rogers, so we will not have an argument now. We will have an argument when you make the application.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I don't mean a hostile witness application. I just indicate that's the way that I'm -- I want to bring him in, see where we go and then we'll take it from there. And if my learned friends want to object to that perhaps they can say so now.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously we would want to be heard before any application were made to treat the witness as hostile, but that's not a submission that needs to be addressed to the Bench now. As regards stage one, that is to say, Mr. Rogers' intention to attempt continue to examine the witness, I make it absolutely clear, there could come a point quite quickly at which I object to that procedure continuing but I don't object to it beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I actually take a slightly different view from Mr. Emmerson here, which is based on the state of the record as I understand it from last night. The witness has made himself clear and if Mr. Rogers is going to ask if he has a change of heart as he put it, and proceed from that basis to make a determination about what he's going to do, whether or not he's going to make an application or not, I have no objection. If Mr. Rogers is going to engage in the same kind of behaviour that he engaged in yesterday without asking that initial question, then I do have an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: On the assumption that Mr. Rogers simply asks the witness whether he has had a change of heart and whether he wishes to answer questions and the answer remains the same and it's taken no further than that, then I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers, prosecute your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I wouldn't want it to be taken that I agree with either Mr. Guy-Smith or Mr. Harvey that my examination should be restricted in the way they seek to restrict it. It's a matter for me how I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Prosecute your case, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kabashi. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, just to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you made at the beginning of your testimony yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, I want to ask you, first of all, when you testified in the Limaj case in 2005, was your memory better then than it is today?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I rise only to -- I rise at this point because of the objection I made previously. It will be a standing objection, so I don't have to continue to rise. I think there is a prefatory issue that needs to be addressed based on the state of the record and where we left off with this witness's testimony yesterday and the state of contention of the Prosecution at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. That standing objection is overruled. Will you prosecute your case, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, I asked you whether when you testified in the Limaj case in 2005, was your memory better then than it is today?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Were the events fresher in your mind, the events about which you testified, were they fresher in your mind then, in 2005, than they are today, in 2011?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I will object to that question as being asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's the exact same question framed in a slightly different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Overruled. Just proceed, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, will you answer my question.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which was your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Were the events fresher in your mind in 2005 than they are today, in 2011?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't get you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Was your recollection about what happened in Jabllanice in 1998 clearer in 2005 than it is today, in 2011?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I rise to make the same objection. The question has now been asked three different times, same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Overruled.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't ... I don't ... I don't know how to answer such questions. Since I'm coming here with my hands cuffed in the same situation I was in the past. In the prison everything is the same, nothing has changed. I can't concentrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, do you accept that in 2005 when you testified you gave a series of answers to a number of questions relating to the events that happened in 1998 in Jabllanice? Do you remember doing that? You were specifically questioned about what happened in Jabllanice, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I was asked questions, but -- but I can't -- I can't make a difference whether it's 2005, 2011. I'm not in a position to give you an accurate answer and I don't want to make mistakes, because I see that the more mistakes you make the more costly it becomes for you. So if it's possible, I would kindly ask you to stop these questions because --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I don't think I am a valued witness for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Let that be the Court's decision. Mr. Kabashi, when you answered questions in 2005, did you answer them to the best of your recollection and ability?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the problem, I don't know how good I was at that time and where I stand now --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I can't tell the difference between the situation at that time and the current situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: When you answered the questions in 2005, did you do so in the best way that you could, trying to remember as well as you could what had happened, to give the Court as honest and truthful account as you could at that time, remembering what you could at that time?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's where the problem lies. I can't recall that time. I can't tell between that time and the present time. I did my best, I hope -- I think to tell the truth because I don't -- I'm not used to lying. But now I really am not in that state of mind as to -- as to clarify things properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying about today --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you really understand me, then please do. There is only one way of understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or do you want me to say something which makes no sense or some word that might cost me dear? I may tell you that I am very pleased to stay in prison and not come so far with my hands cuffed and then go through several checks and so on --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Mr. Kabashi. When you testified in Limaj, you gave a solemn oath, you swore the solemn oath at the beginning, gave a solemn undertaking at the beginning, to tell the truth. Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And when you answered questions following on from that oath, did you answer them truthfully?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, he now -- he is -- he now has answered this question and has indicated that he doesn't know, he can't recall, that's where the problem lies, I can't tell between that time in the present time, I did my best I hope. But Mr. Rogers, again, is asking the same question in a slightly different fashion. It is a sheep in wolf's clothing, and the fact of the matter is we are in no different position than we were at the conclusion of yesterday's proceedings which is why I made the comment at the very beginning of today's proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do think, Mr. Rogers, that question has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I would add that Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith stopped a little bit too soon because Mr. Kabashi also said I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I told the truth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I'm not used to lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's critical.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think if I may say so it's necessary to read back earlier in the transcript because the witness also said I am not in a position -- asked was what you said in 2005 fresher in your memory and more accurate, I'm not in a position to give you an accurate answer, I don't want to make mistakes because I see the more mistakes, the more costly it becomes for you. On a fair reading of the transcript up until now, this witness has said on more than one occasion that he is not in a position to stand over all the detail of what he said in Limaj trial in 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have read that, thank you so much, Mr. Emmerson. Yes, Mr. Rogers, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I would propose to do in light of the answers of the witness is I would wish to tender the Limaj transcript into evidence in this case. Your Honours, I anticipate, we'll have to have an argument about that and it may be that it's better to do that short argument in the absence of the witness. Maybe there won't be an argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There will, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I thought there might. It may be best to do that in the absence of the witness so that he doesn't hear the exchanges going on between counsel as to what he has and hasn't said backwards and forwards. So I would invite the witness to withdraw whilst I make that application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I beg your pardon. I'll say that again. My microphone was not on. Mr. Kabashi, you are excused from the court for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours -- thank you. Your Honours, yesterday when at the -- near to the beginning of, more or less, these proceedings I asked Mr. Kabashi about the Limaj transcript and he gave certain answers. Some of them were his own. First one is at page 385 --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Before Mr. Rogers carries on, could we just be --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Could I make my own application before it's interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Absolutely, but what Mr. Rogers is indicating he wishes to tender the transcript into evidence. Now, so that we can all follow the submissions that he's about to embark upon, because at the moment I'm in the dark and I at least need some clarification. Is he seeking to invite Your Honours to receive the transcript into evidence as evidence of the truth of its contents? Is he seeking at this stage to mount his application to have the witness declared hostile and to cross-examine him upon it with the statement admitted -- sorry, the transcript admitted as evidence of the truth of its contents or precisely what is the application that he is making to which these submissions now go? Because one needs to proceed in logical stages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] As I just said, we will find out if we can just give him an opportunity to make his application.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this isn't the application to treat the witness as hostile or adverse. If it was, I would have started with the phrase: This is an application to treat the witnesses as adverse. It is an application to admit into the evidence in this case the Limaj transcript, as evidence of the truth of its contents. Now that it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Under which rule, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Let me get to it. Your Honours, the witness has stated on a number of occasions that the content of this evidence is true. He said at transcript reference page 385: "What I said in my evidence in the Limaj case and what I'm saying today, yes, I accept that. But for on a number of occasions now I've said that whatever you see in those statements is not true." So he makes a distinction between the evidence in the Limaj case on oath and the statements. And then he -- I asked him a series of additional questions at the bottom of page 385, Your Honour will remember: "Do you stand by what you said in the Limaj trial when you testified before the Court then?" He said: "Yes, on my evidence there, yes. "What you said to the Trial Chamber was the truth, was it, Mr. Kabashi? "A. Yes, on my evidence before the court of law, yes, from what I recall." And then at the end of the transcript, near to the end of the transcript of yesterday at page 401, line 20, when asked whether -- I said this: "Can I ask you this: Is it your position relating to what you said in the trial in Limaj, is what you said in that trial true?" He said: "As I already stated, I'm unable to discuss this further nor to answer more than I have done so far. What I said before this court I accept to my recollection. There are things that I don't remember." Your Honour, we say that this evidence should be admitted under Rule 89. It's relevant evidence, it's probative and can be received under the rules of evidence, 89(C): "A Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value." Your Honours, the evidence goes directly to the heart of a number of the counts. It deals with the associations, to some extent, between the accused and is a clear and consistent account given under oath before a Tribunal of this -- a Chamber of this Tribunal, and can therefore be considered to be reliable at the time that it was made and should be received. It's clearly the case that the witness is having real difficulties remembering today what -- about these events, or so he says. Take it at face value for the moment. I'm not suggesting -- there may be other explanations for that, but taken at face value, for the purposes of this application, it may be that he's having some difficulties remembering, it may be there are other explanations for him saying he doesn't remember. But the fact is this witness has not resiled from his testimony in the Limaj trial and has stated on a number of occasions that it's true. Now, when I asked him about his memory today -- and Your Honours will recall that yesterday it was all about memory-refreshing, and when I took him to a number of parts of the Limaj testimony to ask him if he -- his memory today was refreshed, it was clear from his answers that his memory was not today refreshed. That's at least how he dealt with it. Mr. Guy-Smith objected to me dealing with it in any other way. The value of the answers is simply that he did not remember today about those events. It doesn't mean that the evidence that he gave under oath in 2005 is not reliable and not accurate. Your Honours, so dealing with what he said today I think at transcript line -- page 7, the first few lines, I asked him from the page before: "When you answered the questions in 2005, did you do so in the best way that you could, trying to remember as well as you could what had happened, to give the Court as honest and truthful account as you could at that time, remembering what you could at that time?" And he says: "That's where the problem lies, I can't recall that time. I can't tell between that time and the present time. I did my best, I hope -- I think to tell the truth because I don't -- I'm not used to lying. But now I'm really not in that state of mind as to clarify things properly." So, Your Honours, to -- in our submission, it's quite clear that he believes that he did tell the truth at that time, he said so on oath yesterday twice and more now, and therefore you have the hallmarks of reliability that you require in relation to that testimony. It is relevant and probative directly to the events in this case and should be received. My learned friends are quite entitled to seek to cross-examine this witness on the contents of that statement as to its veracity or otherwise and to explore with this witness in any other way how they see fit their clients' respective cases. And ultimately it's a question of weight for Your Honours, having heard the evidence, having seen and assessed the demeanour of the witness, to determine - having regard to the answers that he's given both to the Prosecution and to the Defence - what weight should be attached to that statement in Limaj, the testimony in Limaj. I'm not seeking to tender any of the other statements, only the testimony under oath. Your Honours, that's my application.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The reason I rose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The reason I rose to interrupt at the outset to ask what the nature of the application was and what rule it was being made under is because Mr. Rogers in the letter he wrote yesterday afternoon in which he set out the strategy he was proposing to adopt today must have deliberately chosen to give the Defence no notice that he was proposing to rely on Rule 89(F) and that's important because there's law on when it's appropriate to rely on Rule 89(F). There is a decision of the Appeals Chamber that says that 89(F) is a lex generalis and that the appropriate course, where a statement concerns the acts and conduct of the accused, is to use Rule 92, either in this context 92 bis or 92 ter. It is not open to a Trial Chamber to rely on 89(F) to admit evidence concerning the acts and conduct of the accused where the evidence sought to be relied upon would not meet the requirements of 92 bis or 92 ter. I'm not in possession --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you keep referring to 89(F). Mr. -- that's not the rule under -- subrule under which Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Rule 89 generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He was very specific, Rule 89(C).

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It makes no difference, the principle is the same. Rule 89 is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's call it by the correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I apologise. Rule 89 is a general provision, it's a lex generalis. Rule 92 is the provision which deals with the admission of any outside court testimony or statement which concerns the acts and conduct of the accused. Why am I not in a position to cite the authority to Your Honours because Mr. Rogers gave us no notice of the nature of the application he was making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, 92, you say 92 bis and 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Shouldn't that include quater, and if I'm not wrong, quinquies?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, it certainly should include both of those, but they're not capable of arising on the facts of this case. 92 quater can't apply because the witness is clearly available and 92 -- he's here in court so to that extent there can be no question about availability.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Mr. Karnavas keeps on trying to intercede. I don't believe that he has any particular voice at this particular time with regard to the application.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: 92 quinquies can't apply because there's nothing that the witness has said that can conceivably meet this requirement. So I've confined what I have to say to 92 bis and 92 ter, and in any event you don't have an application under 92 before you. Now, the Appeals Chamber has held unequivocally that it's not open to the Prosecution to rely on the generalis of Rule 89 if the requirements, the specific requirements of Rule 92 are not capable of being satisfied. So what one needs to do, with respect, is look first at 92 bis and secondly at 92 ter. I'm going to simply say as regards 92 bis that it cannot conceivably apply. I see Your Honour indicating provisional agreement. So one turns to Rule 92 ter. "The Trial Chamber may admit in whole or in part the evidence of a witness in the form of a written statement or transcript of evidence given by a witness in proceedings before the Tribunal under the following conditions: "(A) that is satisfied, the witness is present in court. "(B) the witness is available for cross-examination ..." That criteria is clearly not satisfied. We're not dealing here with a hostile witness. We are dealing here with a witness who has indicated that he is unable or unwilling to testify, and he's not in a position to answer questions on the substance and that applies as much to the Defence as it does to the Prosecution and he's not available for cross-examination. And third condition is that he must attest that the transcript accurately reflects not only his declaration but what he would say if examined before this Tribunal. Now, I want to just pause for a moment. It is absolutely and abundantly clear that those requirements are not met. They're not met because he is not available for questioning on the merits and they're not met because they don't represent the testimony he would give in these proceedings because he hasn't said that they do. Indeed he's said the contrary. I'm concerned that Mr. Rogers stood up to Your Honours to make this application and in doing so he said at page 12, line 3: "It is clearly the case that this witness has difficulties remembering." That is the Prosecution's position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: For the purposes of this application. I made it quite clear, just a moment, you're misrepresenting what I said. I made it quite clear that that was on one view for the purpose of this application that the witness may have difficulty remembering or there may be other alternative explanations as to why he is not answering the questions. Either way those are matters that can be taken into account. It's not right to just highlight one, jump on top of it and seek to suggest that that is the entire basis of my application, which it quite clearly was not and he knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rogers. What Mr. Rogers said at page 12, line 3 that it is clearly the case that this witness is having difficulties remembering. He then, unsurprisingly, realised that that position is entirely inconsistent with his stated intention of seeking to have the witness turned hostile, which is the position he is adopting. He wishes to ride two inconsistent horses and one analysis for the purpose of this application and no doubt a different analysis, inevitably a different analysis, which he's already told us yesterday he intends to pursue in relation to an application he's yet to make. So I understand that Mr. Rogers is uncomfortable with the fact that he said what he said on the transcript and he almost immediately started to backtrack from it, but that is, with respect, because he hasn't a clear line on what it is he is saying in relation to this witness. But be that as it may, the lex specialis is Rule 92 ter, leaving aside the fact that this witness is clearly not available for questioning by the Defence or by the Prosecution, and there is not a situation where he is going to give evidence in substance. He has very clearly attested this morning that it is not the position that he is able to say that what he said in that transcript is the evidence that he would give in these proceedings orally. I just remind Your Honours of the relevant passages. He is asked this morning by Mr. Rogers: "I asked you whether when you testified in the Limaj case in 2005 was your memory better then than it is today? "I don't know." "Were the events fresher in your" -- I'm leaving aside, I'm excising Mr. Guy-Smith's objections as I read the transcript from page 422 on. "Were the events fresher in your mind, the events about which you testified, were they fresher in your mind" -- please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Could Mr. Emmerson, when he cites the transcript reference, could he clearly identify so that we could double-check it, because there have been a number of occasions when what he says has not been accurate. So that we can check the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I thought I'd just given it to you. It's page 4, line 22. Mr. Rogers: "Thank you." I'll go through it again and I'm just going to read it verbatim right the way through not selectively other than to excise Mr. Guy-Smith's objections. "Mr. Kabashi, I asked you whether when you testified in the Limaj case in 2005 was your memory better then than it is today? "A. I don't know. "Q. Were the events fresher in your mind, the events about which you testified, were they fresher in your mind then in 2005 than they are today?" Dropping down from the objection. "Mr. Kabashi will you answer my question. "A. Which was your question. "Q. Were the events fresher in your mind in 2005 than they are today in 2011? "A. I don't get you. "Q. Was your recollection about what happened in Jabllanice in 1998 clearer in 2005 than it is today. "A. I don't ... I don't ... I don't know how to answer such questions since I'm coming here with my hands cuffed in the same situation I was in the past in the prison. Everything is the same. Nothing has changed. I can't concentrate. "Q. Mr. Kabashi do you accept that in 2005 when you testified you gave a series of answers to a number of" -- it says "confessed," it should be questions -- "relating to the events that happened in 1998 in Jabllanice. Do you remember doing that? You were specifically questioned about what happened in Jabllanice. Do you remember that? "A. I know that I was asked questions," says Mr. Kabashi, "but -- but I can't ... I can't make a difference whether it's 2005, 2011. I'm not in a position to give you an accurate answer and I don't want to make mistakes because I see the more mistakes you make the costly it becomes for you. So if it's possible I would kindly ask you to stop these questions." Looking over for a moment at 92 ter(A)(iii), how could that conceivably be regarded as attesting that the witness would say, if examined in these proceedings, what he said in the Limaj trial. Continuing: Mr. Kabashi, after an interruption: "I don't think I am a valued witness for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: "Let that be the Court's decision. Mr. Kabashi, when you answered questions in 2005 did you answer to them to the best of your recollection and ability. "A. That's the problem. I don't know how good I was at the time, and where I stand now, I can't tell the difference between the situation at that time and the current situation." Can I just pause, parenthetically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fact, in fact, while you pause, I'm wondering are you going to reading all that --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to read the relevant passages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you can sort of read a point --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. I was criticised a moment ago for being selective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Anyway --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers was criticising me for being selective. Well then, let me focus in on these, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say to you, Mr. Emmerson, is that you can rest assured the Chamber does have the transcript and we will read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me just be absolutely clear the key passages, first of all, as we've already indicated in the passages I've cited, Mr. Kabashi does not say that he would give evidence in these proceedings in the same terms as he gave evidence in the Limaj trial. He says he is not in a position to stand over what he said in the Limaj trial because he doesn't now know whether what he said is right. He said I'm not in a position to give you an accurate answer. I don't want to make more mistakes -- Sorry, I don't want to make mistakes, because I see the more mistakes you make the more costly it becomes for you. He's already told us that he's made a number of mistakes. He then goes on, a few lines down, to say: "I can't tell the difference between the situation at that time and the current situation." And in answer to the specific question, "Did you tell the Limaj Chamber the truth to the best of your ability," he says, "That's the problem."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will read the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm grateful, but it's important, given that Mr. Rogers is making submission about what the witness's evidence is that I put the key passages on the record. He then asks him: "Did you give evidence to the best of your ability," parenthetically, and he replies: "That's where the problem lies, I can't recall that time. I can't tell between that time and the present time. I did my best I hope -- I think to tell the truth because I'm not used to lying but now I'm really not in a state of mind as to clarify things properly. Now just for the sake of completeness can you just go down to page 12, line 3, and I know that Mr. Rogers took objection to my quotation from him, but just to remind Your Honours. Page -- sorry, page 12 -- page 11, line 23: "Your Honours, the evidence does go directly to the heart" - this is Mr. Rogers - "of a number of counts. It deals with the associations to some extent between the accused and is a clear and consistent account given under oath before a Tribunal -- a Chamber of this Tribunal and can therefore be considered to be reliable at the time it was made and should be received," says Mr. Rogers. And then this: "It's clearly the case that the witness is having real difficulties remembering today what -- about these events or so he says take it at face value for the moment." Leaving that last passage aside, Your Honours, we are in this situation: Mr. Rogers clearly cannot satisfy the requirements of Rule 92 ter, he is not in those circumstances entitled to rely on any general provision in Rule 89. If authority is needed for that it can be sought in a short adjournment. It shouldn't be necessary to have an adjournment because if Mr. Rogers thought he was going to do this, he should have told the Defence so that we would have the authority available to cite to you but the position is very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: For matters of clarity and brevity I join in the remarks made by Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I also join in those remarks, there is only one thing I would like to add which is on a completely different point. I was listening, I don't speak Albanian, don't understand Albanian, but I was listening to the Albanian interpreter and I realise that she is fighting desperately for breath and particularly when people are reading from transcripts we all tend to read rather more quickly and I just as a general reminder to everybody, we do need to slow down a bit when we're reading from transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, when I remember that 92 does not only contain 92 bis and 92 ter, but also quater and quinquies your answer was that 92 quater didn't need our attention because, clearly, the witness was available.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: However, just a few moments ago and it's in the transcript, page 17, line 20, 21, you said that the witness clearly is not available.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, I said he wasn't available for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: For questioning by the Defence and by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He's not available for questioning but he's available to the Tribunal. The terms of Rule 92 quater are clear: "The evidence of a person in the form of a written statement or transcript who has subsequently died and who can no longer with reasonably diligence be traced or who by reason of bodily or mental condition is unable to testify orally may be admitted." He's certainly not dead, he certainly not cannot be traced, he's certainly not unable by bodily condition. If he were unable by reason of mental condition there would need to be evidence. There was no application made under 92 quater so I hadn't sought to address it in my primary submissions. Does that properly answer Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I won't discuss it any further with you, Mr. Emerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Unavailability means he's not capable af being brought into the courtroom and take the oath, and this witness has done both, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers, any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I might, and if I might with regard to the question that you asked, Judge Delvoie, and he has testified in these proceedings orally, which would be another condition under 92 quater. And also since that matter may arise and since you raised the issue with regard to quinquies, also quinquies.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I also say we don't need at this stage procedurally to respond directly to that because there's no application before Your Honours under those provisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers, any response or reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, yes. 89(C). Rules under 89 are important because they provide the Chamber with a fall-back if they require it to ensure that probative and relevant evidence is admitted in the course of the trial and that may be necessary in certain circumstances where the strict provisions of some of the other rules are not met. Now, we would submit that under 92 ter you have sufficient in relation to the answers that were given yesterday to deal with it under 92 ter in any event. Now, I know that under (A)(iii) there appears to be a more specific provision relating to the witness's declaration and what he would say if examined, but Your Honours will know that usually 92 ter is applied at a stage before we reach this particular stage, which is the witness having come viva voce starts to testify and one expects him to testify fully and normally without having regard to 92 ter, 92 ter being at a stage before as we know when we have been dealing with these applications. In an event to avoid the necessity for a witness to have to repeat his evidence as a vehicle of convenience for the Court to receive in a simple way the evidence, as it took to prevent it having to be repeated all over again. That was never the intention with this witness, to pursue an application under 92 ter because it was felt appropriate for him to be here, to be available for cross-examination, and for him to give his evidence orally. He has given evidence orally to some extent, painfully difficult, but nevertheless there are pieces of evidence that have been obtained from him. And we're left in a position with a situation where the Trial Chamber knows that he has given a full account of the events that are the subject matter of this trial. In an earlier time than now when it's obvious that taking simply memory recollections, it's obvious that his recollection then must have been better than it was now. If you look at the transcript, it's quite clear that he gives a series of unimpeded free-flowing answers to the questions that were posed to him at the time. The situation that we're confronted with today is that he, for whatever reason, whether it be genuine or otherwise, has failed to answer the questions relating to what he said previously in any detail, but in our submission, quite clearly, has not resiled from what he said. What he's saying is: I can't remember today and I don't want to confuse myself from today thinking about the situation today as it might have been then. That doesn't mean that his recollection in 2005 was not clear. And Your Honours I think are entitled to assume that when a witness goes into a witness box, takes the solemn oath, and testifies, that they do so in accordance with that oath and to the best of their recollection and ability. To do so -- to fail to do that would be to suggest that witnesses who take a solemn oath don't try to do the things that they're expected to do and the whole criminal justice system all over the world will collapse if we don't start taking some faith in the oaths that witnesses use. Otherwise, there would be no need for them at all. So, Your Honours, it's quite clear if I just refer, if I may, briefly to the transcript in Limaj which is 65 ter 3047 at page 4, when he was sworn, not only was he sworn to testify in the case but he was asked some specific questions about his prior statements. And Your Honours, I'm not seeking to tender those prior statements, but it's significant for how the examination then followed. It said this: "Witness, do you recall that you gave two statements to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor in October and in December of 2004? "A. Yes," he says at page 5 of the e-court reference. "Q. Did you give those statements voluntarily? "A. Yes, after the Prosecutors asked me to give a statement. "Q. And apart from some corrections and explanations which we had discussed earlier this week, were you as truthful as you could be in those statements? "A. Yes." And then they move on into the examination. "Q. Witness, I'm going to directed you now to 1998 ..." and then it begins and the account which flows for quite a few pages of the transcript testimony starts as to how he went to Jabllanice, who he met there, who the commanders were, people who were detained, he names them in detail, and it goes on and on and on, setting out his full account of exactly what happened. Your Honours can see it de bene esse if necessary, it's in the e-court, to look at, to see how he gives his account and decide for yourselves, based upon that free-flowing account, whether in your view he was giving clear recollection to the best of his ability of the events that had happened. Whatever he may be saying today, what was the situation in 2005? Because that is the document that we seek to admit relating to his testimony on that occasion. To exclude it, respectfully, would be to remove from the ambit of this case important evidence about which Your Honours -- relating to the very events about which Your Honours must make a decision. Now, the question of weight is another matter all together. But, Your Honours, we would submit that it would be wrong to exclude it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, before Your Honours take this matter further obviously because we were given no notice we didn't have the authorities available to hand. In the jurisdiction in which Mr. Rogers and I practice it is the duty of counsel on both sides to bring to the attention of the Court authorities which are against them as well as authorities which are in their favour. There are two unequivocal decisions of the Appeals Chamber which hold that the application which is before you now is misconceived and unlawful. The first is the decision of the Appeals Chamber in Galic and the second is the decision of the Appeals Chamber in Milosevic. I'm going to read to you from Milosevic which cites Galic. This is a decision on interlocutory appeal on the admissibility of evidence in chief in the form of written statements. It is dated the 30th of September, 2003 with Judge Pocar presiding, and it cites the authority of Galic. Essentially, the application had been made in broadly similar terms in that case and the Trial Chamber had held that unless the requirements of Rule 92 bis were satisfied, there was no scope for invoking Rule 89(C) which is exactly what is happening here and based on the decision of the Appeals Chamber which is unequivocal in Galic, the Trial Chamber in Milosevic ruled that the statements were inadmissible, the Prosecution appealed, as Mr. Rogers must know and lost. I can just read the judgement for you. I don't have copies for the reasons I've explained. "Issues on the appeal. The first issue for consideration is whether as a matter of law the giving of evidence in chief in the form proposed by the Prosecution is consistent with the rules, assuming that the first issue is answered in the affirmative, then it is requested" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Slow down. I apologise. "Assuming that the first issue is answered in the affirmative, then it is requested by the Prosecution that the Appeals Chamber exercise its discretion and admit the evidence in question pursuant to Rule 89. "Discussion, is the proposal consistent with the rules. "The lex generalis argument. "The Prosecution submits that Rule 89 is not lex generalis to 92 bis," exactly the submission you just heard. "In support of this submission the Prosecution relies on the fact that both provisions were added to the Rule during the 19th revision of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence on 13 December 2000. And upon the reasoning in Judge Shahabuddeen's partial dissenting opinion in a previous application in this case. Then this. Paragraph 9. "The Appeals Chamber has previously dealt with the relationship between Rules 89 and 92 bis in Galic. In Galic, the Appeals Chamber held that Rule 92 bis is the lex specialis which takes the admissibility of written statements of prospective witnesses and transcripts of evidence out of the scope, out of the scope, of the lex generalis of Rule 89(C). In accordance with this decision, where Rule 92 bis is applicable, the requirements of 92 bis must be met in order for the Trial Chamber to admit evidence pursuant to Rule 89." It is with respect, dismay that Mr. Rogers made this application without notice, made it in breach of the clear ruling of the Appeals Chamber did not think it appropriate to bring those rulings to Your Honours' attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Obviously the Chamber would like to reflect on this before it gives its ruling. We will not be able to give this ruling right now, and that being the case the question is: Is there anything that we can do pending the decision or do we have to adjourn?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it would be better if you adjourned, had a look at the authorities, and made your decision as you consider appropriate. It is important because I think it's reached an important stage of the proceedings to determine how we may move next, because if Your Honours decline the application to receive the evidence at this stage, then I will have to move to seek to elicit it, if I can, in another way at this -- so could you deal with it first of all and then make a determination. Your Honours, whatever may be said about 92 bis, this is clearly not a 92 bis case and it doesn't arise in the same way that it would arise under 92 bis or 92 ter. It arises in a very different and very unusual set of circumstances, we submit, that a witness who has come under subpoena and with threat of contempt in other proceedings comes, starts to testify, and then moves away in the way that he did from giving a free-flowing account, when we know that in the past he has given a free-flowing account. So, Your Honours, we don't accept that we are in the same situation that we normally find ourselves in these cases, and that is why rules are broad and capable of broad interpretation to ensure that ultimately justice is done and should not overly restricted. But if Your Honours disagree with that, then of course we understand. But there is -- that is what we say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- submissions and take it from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before Your Honours rise yesterday Mr. Rogers complained to Your Honours that I had made a number of personal criticisms of him, about his professionalism in the conduct of this case. I wonder if for the purposes of the record he wants I'm only giving his opportunity to offer an explanation as to why he didn't cite the two leading Appeals Chambers authorities before you before making an application which they forbid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm rising for slightly a different point. Today Mr. Rogers said at page 24, line 24: "And we're left in a position with a situation where the Trial Chamber knows that he has given a full account of the events of the subject matter of this trial."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, it doesn't say that, sir. Yesterday Mr. Rogers said at page --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yesterday at page 372, line 25 continuing on to page 373, lines 1 and 2, Mr. Rogers said: "Limaj, as Your Honours know, wasn't really about this. This was a small part of the Limaj case and what happened in Jabllanice was not the focus of that trial."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are going to take an adjournment, and the parties will be notified when we can come back. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of August, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 9.59 a.m.,
